title: Egyptian fraction counts and sieve moments
connection: ES shares F04, F12, F21, F22 with counting representations by unit fractions. The transferable object is a count of divisor parametrisations rather than mere existence.
why: A lower-tail estimate for representation counts could turn average abundance into pointwise existence.
first_step: Read Elsholtz–Tao, identify their count parametrisation, and test whether the second-moment argument localizes to prime n.

title: General fixed-numerator Egyptian fraction conjectures
connection: Schinzel-type equations m/n as bounded sums share F01, F02w, F11, F12, F25. The contrast between numerator 4 and neighboring numerators is structurally relevant.
why: A proof technique that exploits a special numerator could clarify exactly which arithmetic of 4 matters.
first_step: Compare the known m=4 and m>4 constructions and isolate the first point where constants cease to be uniform.

title: Four-unit-fraction representations
connection: The four-term Egyptian fraction problem shares F01, F12, F27, F33, while adding a spare summand changes the geometry of the equation.
why: Determine whether a controlled four-term identity can be compressed to three terms using a divisor condition.
first_step: Classify standard four-term constructions by whether two terms combine to a unit fraction and test the resulting divisibility condition for p.

title: Egyptian fractions with distinct denominators
connection: Distinct-denominator variants share F01, F12, F27 and the positivity constraint, but impose an extra exclusion on the ES witness.
why: The extra constraint may expose which parametrisations are robust under denominator collisions.
first_step: Read the distinct-denominator constructions in Graham's survey and check which families permit coincident denominators.

title: Unit fractions with restricted prime factors
connection: Restricted-denominator Egyptian fraction problems share F10, F12, F22, F29: existence becomes a question about allowed divisors in arithmetic classes.
why: A sieve or character-sum treatment of allowed denominators might inform ES divisor selection.
first_step: Search the literature for restricted-prime-factor unit fraction equations and extract the exact divisor-sum identity.

title: Divisor equations in the Erdős–Straus parametrisation
connection: The divisor-sum formulation shares F10, F15, F21, F29. It is a close solved-subproblem family: divisors must lie in a prescribed residue class.
why: Techniques for residue-restricted divisors may provide a pointwise lower bound in the hard splitting case.
first_step: For prime p≡1 mod 4, derive the precise divisor interval and compare with known bounds for divisors in arithmetic progressions.

title: Sums of two unit fractions and multiplication tables
connection: Two-term reciprocal equations share F10, F15, F33 and reduce to factor pairs, much like each fixed-x ES fibre.
why: The elementary factor-pair analysis supplies exact interval and congruence controls for ES slices.
first_step: Write the two-term equation as (a y−b)(a z−b)=c and catalogue the bounds retained when one term is fixed.

title: Sylvester sequence greedy Egyptian expansions
connection: Greedy Egyptian fraction algorithms share F01, F12, F27, F32 but generally increase term count rather than keep it fixed.
why: Their denominator-growth bounds may yield a short certificate or a useful stopping criterion for three terms.
first_step: Check whether the greedy expansion of 4/p ever reaches two residual terms under a congruence-selected first denominator.

title: Function-field Egyptian fractions
connection: Function-field analogues share F01, F12, F26, F27 and replace integer primes by irreducible polynomials.
why: The proof may reveal which steps rely on archimedean size versus factorisation and congruences.
first_step: Locate the function-field ES proof and translate its key divisor-counting lemma to integer primes, marking the exact failed estimate.

title: Unit-fraction equations over polynomial rings
connection: Polynomial-ring reciprocal equations share F12, F13, F26 and often admit algebraic factorisation unavailable over integers.
why: Factorisation patterns can suggest new identities or show why integer size is the obstruction.
first_step: Compare the polynomial proof's factorisation with the integer identity (4x−p)(4y−p)(4z−p) variants.

title: Local-global principles for integral points on surfaces
connection: Integral surface families share F06, F07, F13, F21: local solubility and Brauer–Manin tests may leave integral-point existence unresolved.
why: Integral Hasse principles distinguish a genuine obstruction from a failure of current methods.
first_step: Compare ES's surface with published counterexamples to integral Hasse principles; test whether a descent or torsor formulation exists.

title: Brauer–Manin obstruction in integral-point problems
connection: Integral-point problems share F07, F13, F20 and distinguish rational points from integral points via adelic conditions.
why: Known explicit BM computations can inform whether additional descent invariants beyond ES's known character are worth seeking.
first_step: Read Bright–Loughran's ES analysis and compare its adelic pairing computation with one integral-surface example.

title: Hasse norm principle and norm-form equations
connection: Norm-form local-global problems share F06, F07, F20, F29; quadratic characters encode splitting and local constraints.
why: A norm-form reparametrisation could clarify the role of Gaussian splitting without assuming a new obstruction exists.
first_step: Rewrite the hard p≡1 mod 4 case using norms from Q(i), then compare local-global criteria for the resulting norm equation.

title: Châtelet surfaces and descent by torsors
connection: Châtelet-type surfaces share F07, F13, F15 and may turn a surface-point question into norm equations and divisor conditions.
why: Descent calculations can uncover a parameterisation more effective than a direct search over three denominators.
first_step: Check whether an ES fibre is birational to a conic bundle with a usable torsor descent; derive the smallest fibre example.

title: Integral points on log K3 surfaces
connection: The ES family shares F07, F13, F32 with integral-point problems on affine log K3 surfaces.
why: Height bounds and thin exceptional sets in that area may help explain why small certificates coexist with difficult universality.
first_step: Check the ES surface's classification and compare available integral-point algorithms for the same surface type.

title: Conic bundles and integral fibres
connection: Conic-bundle families share F13, F15, F29 and make each base value a separate factorisation problem.
why: Uniform fibrewise estimates might turn many ES slices into a covering argument.
first_step: Express the ES surface as a conic bundle and inspect uniform integral-point bounds for its fibre discriminants.

title: Vieta jumping for Markov–Hurwitz equations
connection: Markov–Hurwitz equations share F13, F14, F38 and have involutive transformations on integral solution sets.
why: A descent orbit could produce new witnesses from one seed, potentially organizing the ES witness graph.
first_step: Derive the ES coordinate involutions explicitly and test whether any transformation decreases a height function on all positive solutions.

title: Vieta jumping on cubic Diophantine surfaces
connection: Cubic surface Diophantine problems share F13, F14, F38, with solution-preserving swaps or involutions.
why: Height-reducing involutions might explain parity of ES representations and connect otherwise separate solution families.
first_step: Check whether the ES involution graph has a canonical reduced representative for each orbit by minimizing max(x,y,z).

title: Pell equations and thin prime families
connection: Pell-type problems share F02w, F30, F34, often proving infinite but thin parameterized families.
why: A family of ES-valid primes could serve as a rung in a covering system, even without positive density.
first_step: Search Pell parameterisations yielding ES identities and compute the induced prime residue classes symbolically.

title: Polynomial identity methods for Diophantine coverings
connection: Polynomial identity problems share F03, F09, F34, F35: finite algebraic families cover some classes but may provably miss others.
why: Their obstruction proofs could sharpen understanding of what an infinite covering must add beyond finite congruences.
first_step: Formalize ES identity families as polynomial maps and compute the algebraic locus they cover modulo several small primes.

title: Hasse principle failures for affine cubic surfaces
connection: Affine cubic surfaces share F07, F13, F27, where positivity and integrality make rational-point results insufficient.
why: Explicit examples can teach which local-global tools fail to control positive integral points.
first_step: Collect cubic-surface counterexamples with local points but no integral points and compare the missing integrality condition to ES positivity.

title: Integral points and effective height bounds
connection: Effective integral-point problems share F13, F32 and the tension between small certificates and uniform existence.
why: A bound on minimal witness height polynomial in p could permit a structured search or finite reduction.
first_step: Check known effective bounds for integral points on the ES surface and identify whether they are uniform in the parameter p.

title: Rational points versus integral points on cubic surfaces
connection: The distinction shares F07, F13, F27: rational parametrisation need not preserve positive integral coordinates.
why: Studying integral models and denominators can pinpoint why a rationally soluble ES surface remains hard.
first_step: Take a rational parametrisation of the ES surface, track denominator divisibility, and compare with integral-point parametrisations in the literature.

title: Circle method exceptional sets for Diophantine equations
connection: Almost-all Diophantine results share F05, F21, F40: average abundance can coexist with a difficult thin exceptional set.
why: Exceptional-set technology may improve the known density bound or characterize candidate exceptional primes.
first_step: Compare ES's 3/4 exponent proof with circle-method exceptional-set arguments and identify the precise sieve loss.

title: Large sieve for thin exceptional sets
connection: Thin-set problems share F05, F22, F40 and need upper bounds for integers evading every local or combinatorial route.
why: A stronger large-sieve estimate could reduce the exceptional set without proving full pointwise existence.
first_step: Identify the moduli and sieve dimension in the ES exceptional-set argument, then test a larger-sieve bound on the same sequence.

title: Sieve methods for almost-prime values of polynomials
connection: Polynomial sieve problems share F05, F22, F40 and seek pointwise hits in sparse arithmetic sets.
why: Parity-breaking refinements may help where ordinary sieve architecture stalls.
first_step: Translate the ES witness parameter into a polynomial sequence and check whether a bilinear or dispersion estimate applies.

title: Parity problem in sieve theory
connection: Sieve parity problems share F21, F22, F40 and explain why robust average estimates may fail to detect a single required arithmetic type.
why: Diagnosing a parity obstruction can direct effort toward extra structure rather than stronger sieve weights alone.
first_step: Check whether ES's restricted-divisor sequence has a parity-insensitive distribution indistinguishable from a counterexample sequence.

title: Linear sieve and switching principles
connection: Thin sequence sieve problems share F05, F22, F40 and often gain from switching between primal and dual variables.
why: A switching step could exploit the tied parameter/divisor feature rather than treat candidates as an arbitrary sequence.
first_step: Recast the ES divisor condition in both numerator and divisor variables and check whether a switching identity improves level of distribution.

title: Sum-product estimates for reciprocal sets
connection: Reciprocal additive equations share F12, F22, F33 and couple additive structure to multiplication of denominators.
why: Incidence bounds may quantify how many distinct reciprocal sums a structured denominator set can generate.
first_step: Apply an incidence bound to the sets {1/a} and {1/b+1/c} for bounded denominator ranges and compare with required p-scale.

title: Multiplication-table divisor distribution
connection: Multiplication tables share F10, F15, F21: ES needs a divisor in a specific congruence class of a tied integer.
why: Fine-scale divisor distribution could improve over generic divisor-count estimates.
first_step: For the forms 4Cp+1, tabulate divisors by residue class and interval for a bounded sample of primes, then compare with known multiplication-table bounds.

title: Divisors in arithmetic progressions
connection: Residue-restricted divisor problems share F10, F20, F21, F29 and are a direct analytic analogue of the ES witness criterion.
why: Character sums over divisors are precisely the kind of averages whose pointwise shortfall is the ES bottleneck.
first_step: Extract bounds for sum_{d|N, d≡−1 mod q}1 and specialize N to ES's p-tied forms.

title: Character-sum cancellation and genus terms
connection: Character-sum counting shares F04, F20, F21; real characters can dominate while non-real characters cancel on average.
why: An explicit formula for the exceptional character contribution may yield a sharper pointwise criterion.
first_step: Re-derive the count's character expansion and isolate the Kronecker-character term for p≡1 mod 4.

title: Chebotarev and splitting-sensitive Diophantine families
connection: Splitting problems share F06, F29, F36; Chebotarev controls average prime classes but not necessarily a witness for every prime.
why: Separating the distribution-of-primes issue from the per-prime construction can focus the ES reduction.
first_step: List which ES identity families require p split in Q(i), and check whether a compositum's Frobenius classes encode them.

title: Quadratic reciprocity obstructions in parametrised identities
connection: Reciprocity-limited parametrisations share F08, F09, F29: a natural family fails on a quadratic-residue locus.
why: Alternative reciprocity symbols or multiple parameters may cover complementary loci.
first_step: For each known ES family, record its Legendre-symbol condition and test whether two families have complementary failure sets.

title: Covering congruences in prime representation problems
connection: Finite congruence coverings share F03, F29, F34 and build a union of identity families over residue classes.
why: Covering-system optimization might reveal a broader set of usable identities, even if finite coverage is impossible.
first_step: Encode existing ES identity conditions as residue-class sets modulo a common modulus and search for minimal complementary covers.

title: Infinite covering systems by parametrised families
connection: Infinite covering problems share F03w, F30, F34 and replace one finite certificate with infinitely many thin families.
why: A structured infinite cover could accommodate the square-class failures of current finite templates.
first_step: Sort known ES families by prime density and overlap; formulate a criterion under which their union covers all primes.

title: Finite certificate impossibility and polynomial values
connection: Bounded-certificate failures share F09, F35, F36 and show that fixed algebraic templates can miss infinitely many inputs.
why: The obstruction can help identify what additional parameter dependence a successful ES argument must exploit.
first_step: Read the proof of the conditional no-finite-scheme result and list precisely which assumptions fail for infinite or adaptive schemes.

title: Prime gaps and thin algebraic sequences
connection: Thin-family problems share F30, F34, F36 and balance infinitely many explicit cases against no density guarantee.
why: Prime-producing subsequences may be organized via sieve estimates even when proving primality of each parameter sequence is unavailable.
first_step: For a known ES-valid sequence, count primes in its values or identify a guaranteed prime subsequence using established results.

title: Random covering and coupon-collector heuristics
connection: Random covering models share F03, F24, F34; many thin identity families may collectively cover each prime class.
why: A quantitative overlap heuristic can prioritize families with complementary local behavior.
first_step: Estimate coverage probabilities from the actual residue conditions of known ES identities, not independent random assumptions.

title: Poisson heuristics for rare representation counts
connection: Rare-count problems share F04, F24, F37 and model the number of representations as a random variable with fluctuations.
why: A calibrated lower-tail model can identify whether the observed witness abundance is enough to make failures implausible.
first_step: Estimate the mean and variance of the prime witness count from data and compare against a Poisson model stratified by p mod 8.

title: Large deviations for arithmetic representation counts
connection: Representation-count problems share F04, F21, F24 and require a lower-tail bound rather than just a mean estimate.
why: A large-deviation inequality might show that zero representations are too rare to occur at prime inputs.
first_step: Check independence or dependency hypotheses for the ES representation indicators and compute a second-moment lower-tail bound.

title: Linnik-type maximal fluctuations of representation functions
connection: Arithmetic representation functions share F04, F21, F37: average sizes can coexist with exceptional large spikes.
why: Upper fluctuation results warn against replacing a pointwise lower bound with an average or typical estimate.
first_step: Read the maximal-order bound for the relevant divisor sum and derive what it says about ES witness-count fluctuations.

title: Computational proof certificates for Diophantine existence
connection: Certificate problems share F23, F32, F35: a compact witness is easy to verify even when finding one universally is hard.
why: A verifiable finite certificate could support modular reductions or proof-carrying searches over residue classes.
first_step: Design a checker for a residue-class identity certificate and verify its proof obligations independently of the generator.

title: Formal verification of exhaustive congruence arguments
connection: Finite congruence proofs share F03, F23, F32 and can be checked by small proof certificates.
why: A machine-checked database of identities could safely expand the current congruence toolkit and detect missed classes.
first_step: Encode the standard ES Mordell identities and their residue coverage in a proof assistant or a short independently audited checker.

title: SAT/SMT search for Diophantine identity families
connection: Identity-search problems share F03, F16, F32 and turn bounded algebraic templates into a finite search space.
why: Automated discovery may find new identity families, while a symbolic verifier can certify every output.
first_step: Generate bounded-coefficient bilinear/trilinear identities for ES and SAT-search for residue coverage beyond known families.

title: Continued fractions and bounded-length Diophantine representations
connection: Bounded continued-fraction problems share F16, F17, F32 and encode integers through short recurrences.
why: Short-CF classification may produce new finite families of ES certificates or expose the exact exceptional parameter set.
first_step: Translate the ES₅ formulation into continuants and search for a theorem bounding the omitted length-three cases.

title: Continued fractions for rational approximation with congruence constraints
connection: Congruence-constrained short-CF problems share F17, F18, F29 and combine orbit structure with arithmetic conditions.
why: A modular orbit argument may connect short decompositions to the prescribed-entry matrix formulation.
first_step: Express each ES₅ word as an SL₂(Z) product and identify congruence subgroups restricting its entries.

title: Word maps and reachability in SL₂(Z)
connection: Group-word reachability shares F16, F18, F39: ES asks whether a prescribed integer appears as an entry of a short matrix word.
why: Semigroup and Cayley-graph tools could organize valid words and the connectivity of their witness graph.
first_step: Derive generators for the ES matrix words and test whether allowed words form a useful semigroup modulo small moduli.

title: Theta series and coefficient nonvanishing
connection: Theta-series problems share F19, F31, F32: arithmetic representations become coefficients of modular generating functions.
why: Coefficient formulas may isolate congruence obstructions or positivity contributions invisible in the original equation.
first_step: Inspect the ES theta-quotient identity and compare it with modular-form coefficient nonvanishing criteria at prime indices.

title: Modular forms and nonvanishing of Fourier coefficients
connection: Coefficient-nonvanishing problems share F19, F20, F36; analytic average nonvanishing may fall short of every prime coefficient.
why: Methods proving nonzero coefficients in specified progressions could give a pointwise route for ES's generating function.
first_step: Identify the modular object, its Eisenstein/cusp decomposition, and available nonvanishing theorems for the relevant prime subsequence.

title: Quaternion orders and representation of primes
connection: Quaternionic representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime splitting through lattice or order structure.
why: The Gaussian/quaternion reformulation may give a geometric parametrisation of the hard split-prime classes.
first_step: Write the ES quadratic-form reformulation explicitly and compare its lattice with norm representations in a quaternion order.

title: Lattice-point counts on hyperbolas in residue classes
connection: Fixed-x ES slices share F15, F21, F29 with lattice-point problems on split hyperbolas under congruence restrictions.
why: Uniform lattice estimates could bound the number of candidate witnesses in each slice and locate sparse fibres.
first_step: Count factor pairs of the fixed-x product equation in the required residue classes using divisor bounds and compare across x.

title: Bilinear forms in Kloosterman sums
connection: Kloosterman-sum problems share F10, F20, F21 and can control divisor variables tied by a modular inverse condition.
why: Cancellation in the bilinear form may improve distribution of candidate divisor pairs in ES congruence classes.
first_step: Derive the modular inverse relation from an ES divisor parametrisation and check if the resulting sum matches a known bilinear Kloosterman estimate.

title: Additive combinatorics of reciprocal residues
connection: Reciprocal residue sets share F10, F22, F33, where modular inverses combine additively to hit a target residue.
why: Sumset expansion could show that allowed denominator residues cannot avoid all ES target configurations.
first_step: For a prime modulus, compute restricted reciprocal sumsets from the ES denominator conditions and test known sum-product expansion bounds.

title: Graph connectivity of Diophantine representations
connection: Representation graphs share F14, F38, F39: vertices are solutions and local transformations connect them.
why: If each nonempty fibre has a canonical connected component, induction or descent might extend from a set of seeds.
first_step: Construct the ES witness graph under coordinate swaps and Vieta moves for small primes, then determine whether graph invariants suggest a general connectivity lemma.

title: Orbit counting under S3 symmetry
connection: Symmetric representation problems share F14, F38, F04; orbit-stabilizer corrections affect the count of witnesses.
why: Correctly separating generic and degenerate orbits may improve exact counting and parity deductions.
first_step: Compute stabilizers of ES triples and derive an orbit-count identity for R(p), including repeated-coordinate cases.

title: Branching processes for solution-tree growth
connection: Solution-tree problems share F24, F38, F39 and model repeated involutive moves as branching orbits.
why: Tree growth statistics could predict the number of distinct witnesses generated from a seed, while exposing cycles.
first_step: Determine whether the ES transformation graph is locally tree-like at bounded height and calculate its first-return probabilities.

title: Universal Diophantine statements with multiplicative closure
connection: Universal representation problems share F01, F02, F06; multiplicative closure reduces the domain to primes plus local cases.
why: The reduction template may identify a clean prime-only theorem and prevent wasted effort on composite inputs.
first_step: Formalize the ES multiple-closure map and compare it with closure reductions in other universal Diophantine representation problems.

title: Local solubility without integral global points
connection: Local-global counterexamples share F06, F07, F27 and test whether local conditions suffice under positivity and integrality.
why: A catalogue of mechanisms helps distinguish a hidden obstruction from a genuinely hard global construction.
first_step: Compare ES with integral conic and norm-form examples having solutions at every completion but no integral point.

title: Positivity in additive Diophantine equations
connection: Positive-variable problems share F27, F33, F01, while signed solutions can be plentiful and structurally misleading.
why: Positivity-aware methods may yield monotone bounds and compact search regions absent from the signed equation.
first_step: List all sign-sensitive inequalities in the ES parametrisations and test whether they define a convex feasible region for one denominator.

title: Almost-all versus every-input representation theorems
connection: Universal-versus-almost-all problems share F01, F05, F21 and make exceptional inputs the central issue.
why: Methods that eliminate exceptions in neighboring representation problems may indicate what additional arithmetic input ES lacks.
first_step: Compare the proof architecture of an almost-all theorem with a pointwise theorem for a nearby fixed-term representation problem.

title: Function-field versus number-field transfer principles
connection: Arithmetic analogues share F26, F29, F36; function fields often have stronger geometry and different prime distributions.
why: A transfer audit can isolate candidate ingredients that survive specialization to integers.
first_step: Make a proof-by-proof table for the function-field ES variant: identify every use of Riemann–Roch, finite fields, or polynomial factorization.

title: Branching of prime representations by quadratic forms
connection: Quadratic-form representation problems share F29, F31, F36 and encode prime classes through splitting and lattice points.
why: Representation by several related forms might give complementary prime classes analogous to a family-cover strategy.
first_step: List the quadratic forms in ES reformulations and compare their represented prime classes via genus characters.

title: Genus theory and one-sided representation counts
connection: Genus-theory problems share F20, F29, F31 and can explain main terms while leaving a pointwise positive count unsettled.
why: Explicit genus-character decompositions may indicate whether the ES main term is forced or merely expected.
first_step: Decompose the ES count into genus characters and compare the local densities with the predicted main term for each prime class.

title: Residue-class divisor sums and real-character bias
connection: Divisor sums share F10, F20, F37; exceptional real characters can create one-sided fluctuations.
why: Understanding bias helps avoid a false expectation that generic cancellation forces every class to receive a divisor.
first_step: Compute the real-character contribution to the ES divisor count separately and see when it can dominate the error terms.

title: Exceptional primes for parametrised reciprocal identities
connection: Sparse algebraic failure sets share F08w, F25, F30, where a construction works except at explicit exceptional inputs.
why: A classification of failure sets may show that multiple parametrisations leave only a manageable intersection.
first_step: For each ES identity family, factor the obstruction polynomial and compare its prime roots with the failures of sister statements.

title: Prime gaps inside thin congruence-defined families
connection: Thin-family and congruence problems share F03w, F30, F36; families may contain infinitely many primes without positive density.
why: Effective lower bounds for primes in a union of thin families could underpin an infinite-cover construction.
first_step: Check whether any known ES parameter sequences are polynomial or recurrence sequences with established prime-counting theorems.

title: Adelic methods for integral points in families
connection: Arithmetic families share F06, F07, F13, F20; local densities may vary with the parameter and influence global integral points.
why: Uniform adelic analysis could identify parameter classes with systematically stronger integral-point counts.
first_step: Compute local densities of ES surface points at primes dividing 2p and compare with the global expected count across p residue classes.

title: Arithmetic statistics of solution counts in families
connection: Family-count problems share F04, F24, F37 and study the distribution, not just the mean, of integral representations.
why: A distribution theorem could show how exceptional ES primes differ from typical primes and guide a pointwise strategy.
first_step: Estimate moments of R(p) over primes in each relevant residue class and compare with a random model, recording the zero-count tail.

title: Certificate-length bounds and NP-style arithmetic witnesses
connection: Small-witness problems share F32, F01, F23: every positive instance has a short certificate even if universal existence is open.
why: Uniform certificate bounds can make exhaustive search on reduced instances feasible and enable proof-carrying transformations.
first_step: Derive an explicit bound on the minimal ES denominator from known constructions and test whether it is polynomial in p with effective constants.
